record.question:
A bank runs a web application across two Availability Zones. Its TLS private key must be generated inside a company-controlled CloudHSM cluster and must never be exportable to a web server. The architecture must remain available after losing one AZ. Application logs need durable storage, and a separate KMS permission must govern which employees can decrypt them.

Which design meets all requirements?

options.text: Use a TCP Network Load Balancer and copy the TLS private key from an encrypted S3 bucket to each web server during startup. Store application logs in S3 with SSE-KMS and restricted policies.

Use a TCP Network Load Balancer and configure the web servers to perform TLS private-key operations in CloudHSM with a non-extractable key. Spread adequately sized HSM capacity across AZs. Store logs in S3 with a customer-managed KMS key and policies restricting object reads and decryption.
Terminate TLS on an Application Load Balancer using an imported certificate and private key. Store logs on encrypted instance-store volumes and keep the decryption keys only on the instances.
Use a TCP Network Load Balancer and a single CloudHSM in one AZ for TLS operations. Store logs in a private S3 bucket using SSE-S3 and grant authorized employees GetObject access.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. A TCP listener passes the encrypted TLS connection to the web server, whose supported cryptographic integration invokes the HSM for private-key operations. Generate the key as non-extractable and maintain enough HSM and application capacity in surviving AZs. S3 supplies durable log storage; SSE-KMS adds a separate decrypt authorization requirement.

<<1>> creates server-side copies of the private key, violating the custody requirement even if the S3 source is encrypted.

<<3>> moves TLS key custody to the load balancer, and instance-store logs are not durable across instance loss.

<<4>> leaves a single-AZ cryptographic dependency. SSE-S3 does not supply the separately controlled KMS permission requested here.

HSM storage alone does not make a key non-extractable: set the key attribute explicitly. For logs, both S3 read authorization and KMS decrypt authorization matter. Configure TLS clients for HSM redundancy and retry transient failures; merely creating additional HSMs does not prove sufficient surviving capacity.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[CloudHSM TLS integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/ssl-offload.html)
[CloudHSM key management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/bp-hsm-key-management.html)
[CloudHSM availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/bp-cluster-management.html)
[S3 SSE-KMS permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html)

diagram_alt: The TLS key stays inside the HSM boundary; log access passes separate S3 and KMS authorization checks.

sources.supports: Web servers can offload TLS private-key operations to CloudHSM
Non-extractable keys cannot be exported; extractability must be configured
AZ distribution and redundant capacity for HSM availability
KMS decrypt authorization for reads and customer-managed policy control

editorial_notes: Replaced ambiguous corporate-environment wording with an explicit company-controlled HSM boundary and distinct KMS authorization requirement. Added capacity after AZ loss rather than assuming two HSMs always suffice. Answer unchanged.
